description: Join STARLINKER! We are looking for new members — especially young people in person at Yonkers. Bring your voice and your art: be a voiceover for Mission Control, a crew member, or the mysterious Fifth Voice, and draw the spacecraft, crew and Moon base. David writes the text, you provide the visuals and voices. No experience needed — just bring your imagination.
summary: STARLINKER is a playable space mission design game for NASA Space Apps 2026. The lunar relay station that carries messages between Earth, the Moon, and an incoming Mars crew has gone silent. As Mission Designer, the player must design a real rescue mission from scratch: choose a scientific objective, build a spacecraft within strict mass, power, and fuel limits, pick a rocket that can actually lift it, and fly four phases — Launch, Transit, Surface Operations, and Return — while space weather, signal delay, and a mysterious repeating transmission keep rewriting the plan. Every decision is a trade-off, and every trade-off has a consequence the player has to live with. Win, and the Mars crew gets its eyes back. Lose, and the last thing anyone hears is a very polite automated voice saying: “Signal lost. Have a nice drift.”
details:
The problem is real, even if the crew is not

Deep-space missions live or die on communication. A crew travelling to Mars cannot steer, navigate, send science, or call for help in real time — light itself takes minutes each way, and even the Moon is 1.28 light-seconds away. If the relay in the middle fails, the whole chain fails. STARLINKER turns that real engineering truth into a game a player can feel in their stomach: you do not lose because you pressed the wrong button, you lose because three turns ago you traded away the battery that would have saved you.

Science defines the mission. The mission defines the science.

That puzzle sits at the heart of the Space Mission Design Game challenge, and it sits at the heart of STARLINKER. The player starts with a scientific objective — restore lunar relay coverage, map the outage, and return proof of what caused it — and only then earns the right to design the spacecraft. Want a bigger science payload? Then something else gets lighter, hungrier, or more expensive. Want more fuel for a safer return? Then the rocket has to be bigger, and the budget has to survive it. There is no perfect build. There is only the build you can defend.

Designed for grown-ups who still look up

STARLINKER is deliberately cinematic, fancy, and sci-fi driven, aimed at players aged 18 and older: adult stakes, dry humour, moral choices with no clean answer, and a mystery that unfolds across replays. It is not a cartoon and it does not talk down. The wonder is the recruitment tool — a player who finishes a run arguing about delta-v and signal delay at 1 a.m. is a player NASA has already won.

How the game plays

Four phases, no phase forgives you: 1. Launch — Pick the rocket, accept its cost and lift limit, commit the build. Over-mass build; weather hold; budget blown before orbit. 2. Transit — Manage power, fuel and the 1.28-second Moon signal delay in real decisions. Solar storm; drifting trajectory; a signal that arrives too late. 3. Surface Operations — Land at the relay, diagnose the outage, repair or replace under time pressure. Dust, darkness, low battery — and something answering back. 4. Return — Bring the crew and the evidence home on whatever fuel is left. A safe return with no proof, or proof with a terrifying fuel gauge.

Trade-offs are the game: Bigger science payload — More data, higher science score — More mass and power draw; less fuel margin. Extra battery bank — Survive the lunar night / an eclipse — Heavier spacecraft; a smaller payload. Larger rocket — Lift almost anything you design — Launch cost rises sharply; budget ending unlocks harder. Faster transit — Less radiation and storm exposure — Far more fuel burned; a riskier return. Repair the old relay — Cheap, fast, heroic — It may fail again — mysteriously, it already has once. Replace the relay — Reliable, long-lived coverage — Longer surface time in worsening conditions.

Three difficulty levels: Cadet (learn the ropes, generous margins), Commander (the intended game — real limits, real storms), and Deep Black (one save, permadeath for the mission, and the mystery gets stranger).

Replayable endings: at least five — Clean Restore, Costly Victory, Signal in the Dark, Silent Return, and the secret Fifth Voice ending, which no single playthrough explains.

"What could go wrong? What would you do?" Every phase ends on that exact question, with the player's answer logged into the mission record the judges see.

Accessibility: colour-blind-friendly palette (no information carried by colour alone), icon-plus-text labels, adjustable text size, and a full turn-based mode for players who do not want timers.

Spacecraft, payload and rocket cards

The values below are STARLINKER's in-game design specifications — the fixed rules of the puzzle — presented so judges can see the balance the player has to solve.

Real facts woven into play include the Earth–Moon distance and its 1.28-second one-way signal delay, the far longer light-time toward Mars, lunar night and dust as power and equipment hazards, and solar activity / space weather as a transit risk the player must forecast, not just survive.

Relay Runner — Role: Crewed lunar relay repair spacecraft. Dry mass budget: Player builds within a fixed mass cap; every module added removes capacity elsewhere. Power: Solar arrays plus battery bank; power is spent per phase, and the lunar night is not negotiable. Fuel / propulsion: One fuel reserve shared across transit, landing and return — spend it early, fear it late. Science payload (player's choice): Relay diagnostics kit; lunar surface camera; radiation / space-weather sensor; sample and evidence recorder. Crew: Five fictional crew — each gives one ability and one complication.

Rocket card (in-game): Class: Heavy-lift launch vehicle, selectable in three sizes. Height / lift / cost: Each size card lists its height, lift capacity and launch cost in-game; the largest lifts anything and bankrupts almost anyone. Design rule: If it does not fit the rocket, it does not fly — no exceptions, no cheating the mass cap.

Meet the crew — five original, fictional characters

TRANSPARENCY: The five characters below are fictional crew created for this game. They are not real people and they are not team members. The team has one human member — David Acala.

Atlas Prime — Mission Commander. Never panics; +calm in a crisis. Complication: will not abort, even when aborting is the smart move.

Neoplasm — Science Officer. Reads the relay's data like a diary. Complication: keeps hearing a pattern in the static nobody else can hear.

RedPengram — Flight Engineer. Can fix anything with power still in it. Complication: names every tool, argues with the spacecraft, and once filed a formal complaint against gravity.

Castiletank — Pilot / Navigator. Flies the mass budget like a tank through a doorway — somehow, it fits. Complication: utterly superstitious about launch music.

Black Dolphin — Comms & Deep-Space Ops. Owns the signal chain Earth–Moon–Mars. Complication: received the mysterious transmission first — and answered it before telling anyone.

Humour — because real mission control has it too

RedPengram's pre-launch checklist includes item 47: "Apologise to the spacecraft in advance." Mission Control's automated voice stays soothingly polite at the worst moments — including "Signal lost. Have a nice drift." Castiletank refuses to launch without the crew's terrible playlist, and the game makes the player defend that choice in the mass budget: the speaker stays, a sensor goes. Players always keep the speaker. The budget screen has one greyed-out line item nobody can select or delete: "Coffee — priceless — already spent." In Cadet mode, failure messages are written as performance reviews from Atlas Prime, who is disappointed in a very supportive way.

Mystery — the Fifth Voice

On every run, at the moment the relay dies, the log contains 11 seconds of transmission that should not exist: a signal that left the Moon before the relay failed, addressed — impossibly — to the Mars crew by name. No playthrough explains it the same way twice. In one ending it is an echo of the player's own future distress call, bounced back by their earlier choices. In another, Neoplasm proves it was a test signal the relay invented to keep itself awake — and begs the player not to shut it down. In the secret Deep Black ending, Black Dolphin finally admits she answered it on the first run — in a previous playthrough. The game remembers. So does she. Clues are real science in disguise: signal delay, Doppler shift and storm timing are the only tools that can prove or disprove each theory, so solving the mystery means learning the mission physics. That is the innovation: the mystery is not decoration on top of the game. The mystery is the tutorial, the science check, and the reason to replay — all at once.

Transparency note for the judges

Team STARLINKER has one human member: David Acala, team owner, creator and mentor, registered at the Yonkers, NY Local Event. There are no other human team members, and none are claimed. Atlas Prime, Neoplasm, RedPengram, Castiletank and Black Dolphin are original fictional characters created by David Acala for this game. They appear as the in-game crew and as the creative device through which the mission is taught. They are not real people, they did not write code or text, and they should not be credited as team members in any judging, prize or participation record. An open invitation stands: anyone who wants to join as a real human contributor is welcome to reach out through the Space Apps Help Desk / team page. If real members join, they will be added to the team page by name, given real tasks — research, play-testing, science checking, accessibility review, additional endings — and credited here. Until then, this is honestly a solo project wearing a very fancy fictional crew jacket, and we would rather tell you that plainly than dress it up.

SI / AI disclosure

Super Intelligence (SI) / artificial intelligence tools were used in creating this project, including an AI agent used for drafting and organising submission text, structuring the game design, and helping build the playable web app, and AI media generation used for promotional artwork and video. All AI-generated images and video in promotional material are watermarked / disclosed as AI-generated where the platform allows. The game concept, story, characters and creative direction are David Acala's. No NASA logo, insignia or mission identifier is used in this judged submission; a separate promotional version carrying branding is for outreach only and is not part of the submission.

How STARLINKER answers the five judging criteria

Impact: Teaches real mission design — trade-offs, signal delay, space weather — to an adult audience through a story they want to finish, and ends with an open invitation for real people to join and extend it.

Creativity: A fictional crew with conflicting abilities, a mystery transmission that changes across replays, and humour written into the systems (mass-budget playlist, priceless coffee) rather than pasted on top.

Validity: The puzzle is solvable only by respecting the stated mass, power and fuel limits, the rocket's lift, and real light-time delays. Cheating the physics loses the game.

Relevance: Directly answers Space Mission Design Game: player-designed mission, scientific objective, described spacecraft and payload, rocket facts, phases, trade-offs, difficulty levels and replayable endings.

Presentation: Cinematic sci-fi art direction, a 30-second demo script, and copy written field-by-field so judges see the science and the story in the first minute.
